idiom_name: match over a serde-tagged enum (exhaustive), forwarding to per-route channel senders
implementation_notes: Model the messages as an enum and let serde decode the wire tag straight into the right variant (#[serde(tag = "type")] internally tagged - the representation common in Java-style payloads), then route with match: the enum is the routing table, the compiler rejects a missing arm so a new variant cannot be forgotten, and each arm forwards to its own destination sender, for example a tokio::sync::mpsc Sender per route. This replaces both the router object and the runtime predicate list whenever the message set is closed; a Vec<(Box<dyn Fn(&Msg) -> bool>, Sender<Msg>)> remains the escape hatch when rules are configuration-driven or value-based, and the owned-and-decoded message moves into the chosen destination without a re-parse.
code_sketch:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type")]
enum Msg {
    OrderCreated { id: u64, amount_cents: u64 },
    InvoiceIssued { id: u64 },
}

match msg {                       // exhaustive: a new variant breaks the build
    Msg::OrderCreated { amount_cents, .. } if amount_cents > 1_000_000 =>
        review_tx.send(msg).await?,
    Msg::OrderCreated { .. } => orders_tx.send(msg).await?,
    Msg::InvoiceIssued { .. } => invoices_tx.send(msg).await?,
}
pitfalls: Internally tagged enums cannot contain tuple variants (serde rejects them at compile time), so message shapes are limited to struct, newtype and unit variants.
An unknown or missing tag fails deserialization before routing runs, so the unroutable path must handle serde's error, not a match arm.

Sending inside the match with .await applies that route's backpressure to the router: one slow destination on a small bounded channel stalls the routing of every other destination unless each route has its own task or buffer.
